title: GPU inference engine engineering
subtitle: I built a batched continuous-decode engine with paged key-value memory, admission control, canary-gated binding and typed refusals, and I tried the vendor's industrial stack first and closed it on measurements.

stats.label: removed per token by the on-GPU decode loop, up to 696 under load
faster prefill in 256-token chunks, identical answers
CUDA context, reported apart so admission stays honest
less device memory with NVFP4 weights, about 5 percent slower

lede: Capabilities model is a 0.6-billion-parameter tool-discovery model that had to serve two thousand concurrent agents. It had only the memory a resident 30-billion-parameter model left free on one NVIDIA Blackwell GPU. I had the vendor's industrial stack tried first. Its weight conversion corrupted some tensors by up to a thousand times. That is Trying the industrial path first. I can take a model from weights to a custom inference engine whose speed and numerics I can defend. I then directed the build of a purpose-built engine in Rust and CUDA, with its lab. It uses hand-written FP32-accumulating kernels with no cuBLAS and no tensor cores.
quote: I build custom only after measuring the standard option.
evidence: GPU inference optimisation: a purpose-built Rust and CUDA decode engine for a 0.6B tool-discovery model, with the decode loop as one CUDA graph removing 518 microseconds per token.
Deterministic GPU computation: one block per output row and fixed reduction trees, passing 12 of 12 bit-identity gates and 2,345 of 2,345 rank-one results across shuffled batches.
TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM engineering: the vendor stack measured first at 492 requests per second with the card to itself and 56 beside the serving model, before building custom.
LLM quantization: NVFP4 weights using 2.53 times less device memory than FP8 at about 5 percent slower.
author: Corey James
